questions.q: This class compiles in JavaScript. What does TypeScript (strict) say about it?
questions.explain: TypeScript wants every property declared at the top of the class with its type. id is declared and set in the constructor, so it is fine. title was never declared, so this.title is error TS2339, the same error a typo like this.titel would give.
options: Nothing: assigning in the constructor creates the property
Error: property title does not exist on type Task
It only warns, and the program still type-checks

questions.q: Which property does TypeScript (strict) reject, and why?
questions.explain: done = false gets a value and TypeScript infers boolean. id is set in the constructor. title is declared as a string but never set, so it would really be undefined: error TS2564, "has no initializer and is not definitely assigned".
options: done, because it has no type annotation
title, because nothing ever gives it a value
id, because it is assigned after it is declared
None of them: missing values just become undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: complete() returns this, the task itself, so you can call describe() right after it. Each new Task is a separate object, so the second task is still not done.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'describe')

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: All four properties exist on the object, in the order they are declared. Node prints the class name in front of the object, so you can tell a Task from a plain object.
options: Task { done: false, tags: [], id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' }
{ done: false, tags: [], id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' }
Task { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false, tags: [] }

questions.q: Which constructor makes title a property of the object without any other line?
questions.explain: Putting public, private, protected or readonly in front of a constructor parameter makes it a parameter property: TypeScript declares the property and copies the argument into it. A plain parameter is only a local variable.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: All three parameters are parameter properties, so the object gets id, title and done. done uses its default false. title is not readonly, so it can be changed afterwards.
options: Task { id: 1, title: 'Buy oat milk', done: false }
Task { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false }

questions.q: Which line does TypeScript reject?
questions.explain: readonly means the value is set once, in the constructor, and never changes: error TS2540 "Cannot assign to 'isbn' because it is a read-only property". title is a normal public property, so changing it is fine.

questions.q: A property is readonly and holds an array. What does this print?
questions.explain: readonly stops you from pointing saved at a different array. The array itself can still change, just like a const variable holding an array. So push works.
options: TypeError: Cannot add property 0, object is not extensible

questions.q: Why does Node's built-in type stripping refuse parameter properties like constructor(private repo: Repo) {}?
questions.explain: Type stripping works by removing the type parts and running what is left. A parameter property is not just a type: TypeScript has to write the assignment for you. tsx, tsc and the browser terminal do that, which is why the course runs code with tsx.
options: Because private is not allowed in JavaScript
Because they generate code (the this.repo = repo line), and type stripping only deletes types
Because they are slower than normal properties
Because Node does not support classes in .ts files

questions.q: Who may use a protected property?
questions.explain: public (the default) is for anyone, private is only for the class itself, and protected adds subclasses. Outside code may use neither private nor protected.
options: Only code inside the same class
Code inside the class and inside classes that extends it
Only code in the same file

questions.q: Which line does TypeScript reject?
questions.explain: Account may use its own private history, and the subclass Savings may use the protected balance. deposit is public. But outside code reading s.balance is error TS2445: protected is for the class and its subclasses only.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: TypeScript's private is only a type, and types are erased: at runtime passwordHash is an ordinary property, so it goes into the JSON. A # field is private in JavaScript itself and never appears in JSON.stringify.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After compiling, private token is a normal property, so Object.keys lists it. A #token field is not a normal property at all: it is hidden from Object.keys, JSON.stringify and outside code.

questions.q: This file type-checks. What does it print?
questions.explain: TypeScript allows square-bracket access to a private property as a deliberate escape hatch, and at runtime the property is really there. private organises your code; it does not hide anything.

questions.q: A class holds an API key that must never leak into logs or responses. Which is the right choice?
questions.explain: private, protected and readonly are compile-time checks only: at runtime the key is a normal property that JSON.stringify and console.log show. #apiKey is enforced by JavaScript. Even better, build responses with only the fields you choose.
options: private apiKey: string, because TypeScript blocks access from outside
A #apiKey field, and never put the object itself into a response
readonly apiKey: string, so nobody can change it
protected apiKey: string, so only subclasses see it

questions.q: A User object has id, email and a passwordHash. What is the safest way to send the user in an API response?
questions.explain: Listing the fields you send is the only way that stays safe when someone later adds a new secret property. Spreading or stringifying copies every normal property, including a TypeScript-private hash.
options: Build a new object with only the fields you choose: { id: user.id, email: user.email }

questions.q: Which line does TypeScript reject?
questions.explain: Inside the class, this.#hash is allowed. From outside there is no way to reach a # field: the string "#hash" is not a property name of User, so TypeScript reports an error (and at runtime it would just be undefined).

questions.q: What happens with new Shape() when Shape is an abstract class?
questions.explain: An abstract class is only a starting point for subclasses. TypeScript rejects new on it (TS2511). You create a subclass that fills in the abstract methods, and use that.
options: A compile error: you cannot create an instance of an abstract class
It works if Shape has no abstract methods
It creates the first subclass of Shape

questions.q: abstract class Notifier has protected abstract send(to: string, text: string): Promise<void>. You write class EmailNotifier extends Notifier {}. What happens?
questions.explain: An abstract method is a name and a type with no body, and every (non-abstract) subclass must write it. The compiler reports the missing method on the subclass (TS2515), long before anything runs.
options: A compile error: EmailNotifier does not implement the abstract member send

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Notifier decides what the message says (taskDue), and the subclass decides how it is delivered (send). Calling taskDue on a ConsoleNotifier runs the subclass's send.
options: to ada@example.com: [Tasks] "File taxes" is due today
to ada@example.com: "File taxes" is due today
TypeError: this.send is not a function

questions.q: When should you choose an interface instead of an abstract class?
questions.explain: An abstract class shares code: finished methods plus abstract ones. An interface is only a contract: "anything that stores tasks must have these methods". Both are checked at compile time.
options: When you only need to share a contract (which methods exist), not any code
When you need finished methods that every subclass reuses
When you want the check to happen at runtime
When the class has a constructor

questions.q: What does TypeScript report for this code?
questions.explain: implements Clock makes the compiler check the class itself against the interface. A missing method, or a method with the wrong type, is reported right there on the class (TS2416 here).
options: Nothing: the class has a now method, so it matches
An error on now: a method returning string is not assignable to one returning Date
An error only where new TextClock() is used
An error at runtime when now() is called

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A class can implement several interfaces, and implements adds no code at all: it is only a check. At runtime the object has just its own properties, and typeof any object is "object".

questions.q: The repository stores copies. What does this print?
questions.explain: save stores a copy ({ ...task }), and findAll hands out copies too. So changing the original object or a returned object never changes what the repository holds.

questions.q: Why does TaskService take its repository and clock in the constructor, instead of writing new MemoryTaskRepository() and new Date() inside?
questions.explain: If the service creates its own dependencies, it is stuck with them forever. Asking for them in the constructor, typed as interfaces, is constructor injection: whoever creates the service decides which real or fake objects to use.
options: Because classes may not call new inside a constructor
So the caller can pass a different repository or clock, such as a database later or a fake clock in tests
Because it makes the service run faster
Because interfaces cannot be created with new, so TypeScript forces it

questions.q: With dependency injection by hand, where are the real objects (repository, clock, service) created?
questions.explain: Services only know interfaces. The entry file (for example main.ts) creates the real objects and passes them in. That one place is the composition root.
options: In every file that needs them
In one place, the program's entry file, called the composition root

questions.q: interface Clock { now(): Date }. Is const systemClock: Clock = { now: () => new Date() } allowed?
questions.explain: TypeScript checks the shape, not the name. A plain object with the right method is a Clock. implements is only an extra check you can put on a class.
options: Yes: any value with a now() method that returns a Date fits the interface
No: only a class that says implements Clock can be a Clock
No: an arrow function cannot be a method
Yes, but only if you add as Clock

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With a fixed clock, "now" never moves. Call Ada was due a day before now, so it is overdue. Pay rent is due exactly now, and dueDate < now is false for equal times, so it is not overdue yet.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A fake clock lets three days pass instantly. After advanceDays(3) the clock says 4 March, which is after the due date of 3 March, so the task is now overdue. Every run prints the same thing.

questions.q: In tests, what is a fake, like FixedClock or RecordingRepository?
questions.explain: A fake implements the same interface, so the service cannot tell it from the real thing. It is simple on purpose: a clock that stands still, a repository that just records what was saved.
options: A copy of the service with the business rules removed
A simple stand-in that implements the same interface as the real dependency
A test that is allowed to fail
A subclass of the service under test

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The recording fake shows exactly what the service saved: trimmed titles, and nothing for the empty one. The test can check repo.saved directly.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: #nextId++ returns the current value, then adds one. Each object has its own counter, so b starts at 1 again. The # field stays out of the JSON.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Counts are kept per e-mail address, so Bob starts at 1. After reset, Ada starts again from 0, so the next hit returns 1. The #counts map is invisible to JSON.stringify.

questions.q: The practice solution gives ReminderService a function () => Promise<string[]> instead of the whole TaskService. Why?
questions.explain: A dependency can be a function type, not just an interface. The reminder service only needs "give me the overdue titles", so a test can pass async () => ["File taxes"] without building a whole task service.
options: Because classes cannot be passed to constructors
Depending on the smallest thing you need makes the service easier to test and reuse
Because functions run faster than methods

questions.q: Wiring services by hand in main.ts works for three classes. What helps when a backend has dozens of services?
questions.explain: A container creates the services in the right order and passes each one what it needs. It works with exactly the same constructor-injected classes; only the wiring moves out of your hands.
options: Making every service create its own dependencies with new
Putting all services in one global object that everyone imports
A dependency injection container, such as @zudojs/container, which does the wiring for you

questions.q: Finish the class Point using parameter properties: x and y are readonly numbers. Add a method distanceTo(other: Point): number that returns the straight-line distance (use Math.hypot). The program should print 5.
questions.explain: constructor(readonly x: number, readonly y: number) {} declares and fills both properties. Math.hypot(3, 4) is the length of the line between the points: 5.

questions.q:
Finish VisitCounter. It keeps a count in a real private # field. visit() adds one and returns the new count; total() returns the count. The count must not show up in JSON.stringify. The program should print:

1 2 2
{}
questions.explain: A #count field is hidden by JavaScript itself, so JSON.stringify gives {}. With private count the output would be {"count":2}.

questions.q:
The abstract class Shape has an abstract method area() and a finished method describe(). Write the subclasses Rect (width and height) and Circle (radius). You do not need to round: describe() already does that. The program should print:

rect: 6.00
circle: 3.14
questions.explain: Each subclass calls super("rect") or super("circle") to set the name, and writes its own area(). describe() is shared code from the abstract class.

questions.q: Write MemoryNoteRepository implements NoteRepository. Keep the notes in a private #notes Map by id. save stores the note (a new save with the same id replaces it); findAll returns all notes. The program should print [ 'Buy oat milk', 'Call Ada' ].
questions.explain: A Map keyed by id replaces the old note when the same id is saved again, and keeps the first position. Storing and returning copies ({ ...note }) stops callers from changing the stored notes by accident.

questions.q: Finish CouponService. It gets a Clock by constructor injection (a private readonly parameter property). isValid(expiresAt: Date) returns true while the clock's time is before expiresAt. Then finish the fake FixedClock so the test prints true false.
questions.explain: The service never calls new Date() itself; it asks its injected clock. That is why the test can check both "before" and "after" instantly, with the same result every run.

questions.q:
Write a fake FakeNotifier implements Notifier that stores every message in a readonly sent: string[] array instead of sending it. The program should print:

2 [ 'Pay rent is overdue', 'Call Ada is overdue' ]
questions.explain: The fake has the same send method as a real e-mail notifier, so ReminderService accepts it. Instead of sending, it records the messages so a test can check them.
questions.expected: 2 [ 'Pay rent is overdue', 'Call Ada is overdue' ]

questions.q:
Finish Wallet. The balance lives in a #balance field starting at 0. deposit(amount) throws an Error with the message amount must be positive when amount is 0 or less; otherwise it adds the amount. balance() returns the balance. The program should print:

amount must be positive
50
questions.explain: Because #balance is truly private, the only way to change it is through deposit, and deposit checks the rule. Outside code cannot write wallet.balance = -1000 by accident or on purpose.

questions.q: Write a generic class Stack<T> with a private #items: T[] array, push(item: T): void, pop(): T | undefined and a size method. The program should print c 2.
questions.explain: A class can have a type parameter just like a function. new Stack<string>() makes T a string, so pushing a number would be a type error. pop() returns T | undefined because the stack may be empty.

questions.q: A User class keeps a password hash. Finish toPublic(user): return a new object with only id and email, never the hash. The program should print {"id":7,"email":"ada@example.com"}.
questions.explain: private passwordHash would still appear in JSON.stringify(user). Building the response by listing the fields you want is the safe habit: a secret added later never leaks by accident.

questions.q: Account has a protected balance. Finish the subclass SavingsAccount with addInterest(rate: number): void, which adds balance * rate to the balance. The program should print 110.
questions.explain: A subclass may use a protected property, so this.balance works inside SavingsAccount. Outside code still reads it through the public current() method.
